name: Egocentric bias
statement: People claim a larger share of a joint effort than the other contributors grant them, so the shares collected from a group sum past the whole.
meaning: The claim is about allocation, not about self-flattery. Everyone in a group has better access to what they did than to what anyone else did, and if the share each person claims is read off that private record, the shares will not fit inside the whole. The test is arithmetic rather than psychological: collect a claim from every member, add them up, and compare the total to 100%. Ross and Sicoly proposed availability as the mechanism, following Tversky and Kahneman and the availability heuristic, entry no. 38: ease of recall stands in for frequency, and one's own contributions come to mind first. They quote the 1973 definition, 'the ease with which relevant instances come to mind', and say plainly that they have no definitive evidence the one bias causes the other.

origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Five experiments on married couples, two sets of laboratory dyads, intercollegiate basketball players and graduate students, testing recall and responsibility together rather than separately. The abstract also names naturally occurring discussion groups, but those belong to a pilot study of a seminar and of pairs talking in cafeterias, not to any of the five.

evidence: Experiment 1 recruited 37 married couples living in student residences and asked each spouse privately to divide responsibility for 20 activities, from making breakfast to causing arguments. Husband and wife each marked a 150-mm line running from 'primarily wife' to 'primarily husband', so a couple whose two marks summed above 150 units had at least one partner over-claiming. The mean excess was 4.67 units, F(1, 35) = 12.89, p < .001, and 27 of the 37 couples showed some overestimation. Over-claiming appeared on 16 of the 20 items on average, including the unflattering ones: causing arguments gave F(1, 32) = 20.38, p < .001. No item showed significant underestimation. The same questionnaire asked spouses to write examples of each side's contributions, and they produced more of their own, 10.9 against 8.1, F(1, 35) = 36.0, p < .001. The size of a couple's recall gap correlated with the size of its responsibility gap, r(35) = .50, p < .01. The other studies change the measure rather than repeat it. Across 12 intercollegiate teams, 119 of 158 basketball players named a turning point caused by their own side against 16 who named the opposition, 13 who named both and 10 who did not answer. Players gave 1.79 reasons for the result involving their own team against 0.09 involving the other, F(1, 11) = 272.91, p < .001. That is a count of what came to mind, not a set of shares added against 100%. In Experiment 5, 29 graduate students were asked about their undergraduate theses in one of two wordings. Those asked about the supervisor gave the supervisor 33.3% of the whole research effort, against 16.5% from those asked about themselves, F(1, 27) = 9.05, p < .01. The second figure is not what anybody wrote down: the authors subtracted each self-claim from 100 and assumed the rest belonged to the supervisor.

replication.headline: Schroeder, Caruso and Epley put 339 museum visitors into handgrip teams of three or six, and the shares they claimed summed past 100% in both sizes.
replication.detail: Each member squeezed a counting handgrip for one minute, then estimated the share of the group total they had produced. Three-person groups summed to 104.0%, six-person groups to 113.6%, F(1, 73) = 4.44, p = .04, partial eta squared 0.06. Three groups were dropped where a member skipped the question, and the analysis ran at group level. The three-person figure sits beside the 103.1% that these authors compute for Ross and Sicoly's married couples, so the size of the original result survives a task whose real shares a counter recorded. Group size drove claims and not work: grips per member did not differ by group size or condition. Asking people to rate the others before themselves cut the sum from 114.8% to 102.6%, F(1, 73) = 7.13, p < .01. An online study of 1,962 people recalling real groups carried the pattern to larger sizes, where groups of five to ten implied 171.0% against 141.1% for groups of two to four. The paper's two field pieces are weaker support than they look. One surveyed 699 MBA students; the other is a re-analysis of the authorship data of Caruso, Epley and Bazerman, so it is not independent of the extension cited below, and in it the group size effect held in the control condition and not in the other-focused one.

study.cite: Schroeder, J., Caruso, E. M., & Epley, N. (2016). Many hands make overlooked work: Over-claiming of responsibility increases with group size. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 22(2), 238-246.

limits: Ross and Sicoly did not show that the recall bias causes the responsibility bias, and say so: the supporting evidence is one correlation in the marriage study and one retrieval manipulation in Experiment 5. Their Experiment 4 tried to shift attention by having 40 men take notes on either their own contributions or their partner's, and the manipulation moved nothing, all Fs < 1, while the over-claiming stayed strong. The samples were small and local, 37 couples and 29 graduate students among them. A laboratory attempt to separate the two ingredients came out against the self-other half. Stinson, Kagan and Pooresmaeili had 51 people compare physical effort in a task where the comparison partner's performance was secretly the participant's own recording, and found no self-other bias, mean -0.027, t(50) = -0.44, p = 0.665, but a reliable bias favouring the trial they had performed over the trial they had watched, mean -0.275, t(50) = -2.75, p = 0.016, d = 0.46. Debiasing has a price. Caruso, Epley and Bazerman ran four experiments in which considering others' contributions cut egocentric claims. Members who had contributed most were then less satisfied, and less interested in collaborating again, than members who had contributed least, and the split was sharpest in cooperative groups.
misreadings: The story usually told is that Ross and Sicoly asked spouses what percentage of the housework they did and the two answers added to well over 100. The experiment proper used no percentages. A footnote explains why: percentage estimates in the pilot interviews were remembered and then compared afterwards, which set the couples arguing, so the published study used unmarked 150-mm lines that subjects could not convert. Retellings also inflate the size. The paper calls the overestimation 'relatively small' and notes that most marks sat near the halfway point, and the excess was 4.67 units out of 150. The bias is not the self-serving bias, entry no. 109, wearing a different hat. It applied to causing arguments and making the house messy, and it appeared in a handgrip contest where no one's self-worth is at stake. It is also distinct from the false consensus effect, entry no. 10, which is about projecting your own choice onto other people's, and from the spotlight effect, entry no. 22, which is about how much attention you think you are getting. This one is about who gets the credit. Yamashiro and Roediger show the same availability account working at group level. Residents of three American states who listed only other states' historical events inflated their own state's share of national history less than residents who listed events for every state, an index of .06 against .10, though the inflation survived the manipulation.
